items.stem: Why can regular expressions alone not parse nested, balanced parentheses?

options.text: Balanced nesting requires counting/memory beyond the power of regular languages
options.rationale: Correct: arbitrary nesting is context-free, not regular, so it needs a stack-based parser.

options.text: Regular expressions cannot match the '(' character
options.rationale: They can match any character, including parentheses.

options.text: Parentheses are reserved tokens that lexers skip
options.rationale: Lexers tokenise parentheses; the issue is grammatical power, not skipping.
The limitation is expressive power, not speed.

items.explanation: Correct: arbitrary nesting is context-free, not regular, so it needs a stack-based parser.

items.stem: Which statements about compiler phases are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens
options.rationale: Correct: the lexer turns the character stream into tokens.

options.text: Semantic analysis checks scopes and types using a symbol table
options.rationale: Correct: it validates meaning after parsing produces a tree.
Parsing builds a tree; code generation comes later.
Optimization operates on an IR produced after parsing.

items.stem: What is an abstract syntax tree (AST)?

options.text: A tree representation of program structure with syntactic noise removed
options.rationale: Correct: the AST captures the essential structure for later phases, dropping punctuation detail.

options.text: A list of raw tokens from the lexer
options.rationale: Tokens are a flat stream; the AST is a structured tree built by the parser.
The AST is an internal representation, not target code.

options.text: A table mapping registers to variables
options.rationale: That describes register allocation, not the AST.

items.explanation: Correct: the AST captures the essential structure for later phases, dropping punctuation detail.
